title: Schools in Italy, Scotland and Northern Ireland hit by threats in suspected bomb hoax
description: Some 6,300 schools across Italy and more than 700 in Scotland and Northern Ireland have received bomb threats, according to local authorities.In Italy
body: Some 6,300 schools across Italy and more than 700 in Scotland and Northern Ireland have received bomb threats, according to local authorities.In Italy a number of buildings were evacuated as a precaution but Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni said checks so far had not indicated any evidence of "concrete danger"."These reports appear rather linked to a strategy intended to cause alarm and concern," she said on Facebook. Scotland's education secretary Mairi McAllan said there was no risk to the public and specialist cyber-crime officers were working to identify the source of the messages. In Northern Ireland education officials told schools to remain open unless otherwise advised by police.It is unclear whether the incidents are connected."As a parent and as a constituency MSP I understand just how concerning this will be for parents, for pupils, for carers and for school staff," McAllan said.Scottish police had earlier said that the warnings were "immediately assessed" as hoaxes. However some local authorities confirmed that some schools had been evacuated."Our advice is that there is no requirement to evacuate schools or keep children away from education based solely on the content of the emails," Police Scotland said.Italian officials said a single email appeared to have been sent on Wednesday to the inboxes of 6,300 out of a total of 7,476 state schools, and private schools were unaffected.The message, said to be from a certain "Mikhail Andropov, leader of Vilayat di Misoginistan", caused alarm in many schools.The BBC has seen the email sent to Scottish schools which appeared to have similar wording, and also referenced the name Mikhail Andropov, although as leader of a "Red Owl" project.Italy's Education Minister Giuseppe Valditara said the incidents involving Italian schools were probably a "cyber-attack, not a genuine risk", adding that there appeared to be a clear strategy behind the rash of threats in across Europe targeting flights, supermarkets and even hospitals.Italian airports along with airlines elsewhere in Europe were hit by a series of bomb hoaxes last week that prompted a series of scares, evacuations and widespread disruption. Although a number of threats were claimed by an extremist misogynistic group, it later denied any link to the false warnings.On Wednesday one Milan headteacher, Anna Bertato, told Italian media she had checked the email address of the sender online: "It was already classified as spam by a student at a university in Taiwan."Another Milan headteacher, Massimo Nunzio Barrella, told Adnkronos news agency that he had immediately realised the email was spam when it arrived in his inbox at 08:59 and he decided not to evacuate his school and reassured parents who phoned in."The text seemed almost comical," said Barrella, "it was like a message from Martians: 'We have come to annihilate you.' I even had a bit of a laugh."Although many schools were initially evacuated on Wednesday, the alarm was quickly lifted, and pupils were allowed to return to class. Some parents decided to take their children home for the day, but the majority of schools in Milan did not send their pupils home.Some 280 school head teachers had already received threats in recent days, according to Italian reports.In a statement, the head of the central Umbria region Stefania Proietti said "checks conducted so far in Umbrian schools have proved negative, and law enforcement is working rapidly and carefully to verify each report".

schema.headline: Schools in Italy, Scotland and Northern Ireland hit by threats in suspected bomb hoax

title: Jess Phillips calls for phone tech to block live-streamed child sex abuse
description: Former safeguarding minister Jess Phillips has joined calls from campaigners for the government to back new technology that blocks the live-streaming
body: Former safeguarding minister Jess Phillips has joined calls from campaigners for the government to back new technology that blocks the live-streaming of child sexual abuse.The UK National Crime Agency has flagged the UK as the third biggest market in the world, external for live-streamed abuse, where children are sexually abused live on camera to order.Device-level blockers can prevent this material being filmed and viewed on smartphones, laptops and tablets in the first place, Phillips said, at the launch of a policy report in Parliament.Anti-abuse campaigners claim keeping the technology at device level maintains privacy and encryption. Civil liberties campaigners Big Brother Watch dispute this. The government has already legislated to demand tech firms like Apple and Google, which develop the operating systems of most smartphones used in the UK, block under-18s from taking or sharing nude images on smartphones and other devices.However, three-quarters of child sexual abuse material (CSA) was not self-generated but likely captured on adult devices, according to 2025 research from the Internet Watch Foundation (IWF), which works to eliminate child sexual abuse imagery online.Some 1.8 million men in the UK admitted to some form of online sexual offending against children, according to research from child safety institute Childlight. Phillips, who complained of repeated delays to work to tackle CSA when she resigned as safeguarding minister in May, is demanding action to tackle the source of the crime and reduce the number of British offenders. "This should be a source of national shame, and we must stop it," the Labour MP said."The technology, the evidence and the public support are all there - I want to work with ministers to extend on-device blocking to child sexual abuse material on every device sold in Britain, making children here and over the world safer."The software uses AI to classify known child abuse images in the phone's operating system, and blocks the material at the moment it is viewed or created, whatever app is in use.Nothing is logged, stored or sent anywhere, and the tech would work alongside encryption.The AI classifier has been trained against a database of known child abuse images so it can differentiate between harmless material such as children at the beach, and sexual abuse.Phillips said online child sexual abuse is "an issue that we did not keep control of" as legislators and now must be prioritised, at the event in Parliament.She was joined by survivors of online child sexual abuse, who said they should not have to beg for the removal of images of themselves being abused from the internet.Phil Eccles, from the National Crime Agency (NCA), said the scale of the problem was "at crisis point"."This would cut off at source somebody on the UK their ability to direct a live stream for a child to be abused," he said."To me, safeguarding children will always supersede the ability to prosecute. If we can stop that abuse we must."But it's so important that tech companies come onboard - we cannot arrest our way out of this problem."The parliamentary briefing also heard from the former minister, Conservative Lord Nash, who led the campaign for an under-16s social media ban.He said: "By the time the police are involved, a child has already been abused and the images and videos have gone round the globe."The material has to be blocked on the phone itself, before the harm is done."The government deserves real credit for committing to exactly that on children's phones."I urge it now to extend that commitment to every device sold in Britain, targeted at CSA material, and to lead the world in doing so."In a sign of CSA becoming more prevalent, communications watchdog Ofcom has found almost as many offenders looking for CSA on everyday apps on the open web as on the dark web.John Tanagho, from the anti-trafficking organisation the International Justice Mission, highlighted how children in poorer countries were being targeted for sexual exploitation, with research showing one in every 100 Filipino children were victims.Legislation should explicitly limit the scans to identifying and blocking CSA material, he said, with no data shared with the government or any private companies, maintaining privacy.However, civil liberties campaigners Big Brother Watch warned about the possibility of innocent images being blocked or the technology being adapted for surveillance in future."Effective child protection requires a stronger criminal justice response," a spokesperson said. "Yet police are already overwhelmed by reports of child sexual abuse, while the NCA has rightly raised concerns that eight in ten offenders convicted of possessing child abuse images avoid prison."Genuine child protection requires well-resourced, targeted policing and robust enforcement of the law, not the scanning of every phone in Britain."A government spokesperson did not respond directly to the new call for CSA blockers, but said: "We are putting in place the strongest online safety laws in the world."This includes preparing world-first legislation to call on the biggest technology companies to make it impossible for children to take, share or view nude images."We will also give the police the powers they need to keep pace with criminal use of emerging technologies in order to keep our children safe."

schema.headline: Jess Phillips calls for phone tech to block live-streamed child sex abuse

title: Police helped remove Russell Brand after 'violent incident' at Jemima Goldsmith's home
description: Police have confirmed they helped Jemima Goldsmith to remove ex-boyfriend Russell Brand from her property in 2014 after she claimed a violent incident
body: Police have confirmed they helped Jemima Goldsmith to remove ex-boyfriend Russell Brand from her property in 2014 after she claimed a violent incident took place.Thames Valley Police said officers were contacted by an alleged victim and went to an address in Oxfordshire on 25 July 2014 but no arrests were made.They listened to her concerns and gave support, and "also ensured the victim's partner left the address, as per the victim's wishes", the police added in a statement on Wednesday.Goldsmith, who dated Brand for about a year, wrote on X on Monday that she "had to call the police to have him removed from my house in 2014 during a violent incident" but chose not to press charges.Brand was jailed for 10-and-a-half years for rape and sexual assault on Monday.In her post, 52-year-old Goldsmith, who wasn't part of the trial, said she was "in awe of the courageous women who came forward at Brand's trial" and was "glad and relieved" he had "finally faced justice".She wrote: "I have had my own personal experience of his violence, coercive control and abuse."I had to call the police to have him removed from my house in 2014 during a violent incident."The Press Association reported that Goldsmith had asked for Brand to leave the property, her wish was then communicated to him by police, and he agreed to leave the house.Goldsmith added: "I chose not to press charges at the time and not to go public with this, as I was worried about the impact of the press attention on my then teenage children."I have neither seen nor spoken to Brand since that period in 2014. Whilst my pain in relation to this, pales in comparison to what the women have testified in court have suffered, this was a difficult period in my life which has had a lasting impact."She also said she had "assisted the journalists who finally exposed him", and had been willing to testify to his "abusiveness" if they were sued.TV producer Goldsmith is also the former wife of ex-Pakistani prime minister and cricketer Imran Khan, the daughter of late billionaire entrepreneur Sir James Goldsmith and sister of ex-Conservative government minister Zac Goldsmith.

schema.headline: Police helped remove Russell Brand after 'violent incident' at Jemima Goldsmith's home

title: What is the state of our grooming laws?
description: Time and again since the international explosion of the "Me Too" movement in 2017 against sexual violence against women and girls, politicians have be
body: Time and again since the international explosion of the "Me Too" movement in 2017 against sexual violence against women and girls, politicians have been pushed on whether we in the UK have an adequate list of crimes in place to deal with all manner of incidents.Those demands for reviews and rethinks have come back again with the conviction of one comedian Russell Brand for rape and sexual assault - and separate accusations of sexual misconduct against another one, David Walliams. He denies being a sexual predator and is not facing a criminal investigation.The modern landscape of sexual offences in England and Wales is complicated - but it is far more nuanced than it once was because of major changes over the last two decades.There is some confusion in public debate over what counts as grooming - but in general it's understood in the criminal courts to refer to situations where a predator builds a relationship of trust with a child target in order to prepare the ground for sexual activity. Given the end goal, that relationship will often involve a great deal of manipulation - usually emotional, often subtle and regularly coercive.Since 2003 it has been an offence for an adult to meet a child "following sexual grooming" and the maximum sentence is 10 years.The crime is committed when an adult has met or communicated with someone under 16-years-old on at least one occasion and then intentionally meets them, or travels to meet them, with the intention of committing a sexual offence.There are other offences which generally cover some of the ground of grooming: arranging and facilitating a child sex offence, sexual communications with a child, causing a child to watch a sexual act or inciting an under 13-year-old to take part in one.The offence gets little media attention, but analysis from the Centre of Expertise on Child Sexual Abuse, an independent body funded by the government to provide insights, shows that grooming offences are regularly turned to by the police and prosecutors.Its latest report on crime statistics shows that 7,197 sexual grooming offences were recorded by the police across England and Wales in 2024/25.Nearly a third of those ended up in a charge - and in 2024 just over 2,000 defendants were convicted.  The rate of prosecuting suspects for grooming has more than doubled in seven years.One final offence to highlight is the crime of abusing a position of trust for a sexual purpose with a child. This covers young people up to the age of 18 because the abuse may be taking place in a care environment.Since June, grooming has been a specific element of sentencing law. Judges who are deciding a sentence for a child sex offender to consider how the contact came about - and if there was evidence of grooming, that becomes a factor to increase the length of the sentence.So does that mean that the law is entirely settled and accepted? Well not quite.Some campaigners have been calling for the law to clearly define what grooming means. ThirtyOne:Eight, a charity consultancy that works on improving safeguarding in religious settings, said last year that its work had led it to conclude that the intention to groom - whether or not sexual abuse takes place - should become a self-standing crime.And Baroness Louise Casey, who carried out a national audit of grooming gang abuse, highlighted another issue.Sexual offences law includes a subtle exception for teenagers who have not yet reached the legal age of consent at 16 but who are in a relationship with each other. That nuance is designed to avoid needlessly criminalising 13 to 15-year-olds who seemingly know what they are doing.But, says Casey in her report, there were "examples of perpetrators being charged with the lesser offence of 'sexual activity with a child', rather than rape, because of a belief that the child involved had 'consented' to having sex."Speaking to the BBC Radio 4's Today Programme, she said that it was "staggering" that adults who have sex children aged 13, 14, and 15 are not automatically charged with rape, as is the case in France.She has asked for that gap to be closed and told the BBC she had received an assurance from ministers this it would happen."The recommendations from the grooming gang audit that I did last year are works in progress," she said. "They're not completed yet, and obviously, I would like the government to press on with those."The Ministry of Justice has been contacted for comment.All of that is aimed at dealing with crimes against children and young teenagers. So is there space for changes elsewhere?Some argue that the UK should have a "staggered" age of consent.This became a talking point in 2023 after allegations against Russell Brand exploded over the media.One of his alleged victims told BBC's Woman's Hour at the time that we should consider changing the law so that people over 18 would not be allowed to have sex with 16 and 17-year-olds."There's a reasonable argument [that] individuals between the ages of 16 and 18 can have relations with people within that same age bracket," she said. "You're allowed to make mistakes as a teenager, they should be with other people your own age."The counter-argument to that is once someone is over the age of consent, the law already makes clear that they have the maturity to consent to sex. And if they have not given it, the law is clear: the act is not one of love, but rape.

schema.headline: What is the state of our grooming laws?

title: Why does Australia want Brits to swap Sydney for the outback?
description: In a Mexican restaurant in north-east Australia, the tacos are served by staff from France, Italy, Ireland and Argentina.Cairns has long attracted a y
body: In a Mexican restaurant in north-east Australia, the tacos are served by staff from France, Italy, Ireland and Argentina.Cairns has long attracted a young and transient international crowd, who enjoy the tropical lifestyle while earning money for travel.But one nationality is in shorter supply than it used to be."You get far fewer British backpackers looking for jobs here these days," says Mexicairns owner Peter McLeay.It's a trend McLeay has noticed since mid-2023, when a free trade deal between the UK and Australia kicked in.That agreement - as well as tariff-free trade in Tim Tams and Penguins - included special treatment for Brits on working holiday visas: exemption from having to find jobs in regional or remote places if they wanted to remain beyond a year.That, along with an increase in the age limit from 30 to 35 saw backpacker visas issued to Brits surging from 47,200 in 2023-24 to just over 77,000 in 2025-26, according to the latest Australian government data.Without the incentive to go regional, many are choosing to base themselves in the big cities, or, according to Prime Minister Anthony Albanese, "Bondi or Coogee" - two of Sydney's most famous beachside suburbs.Now though, with Brits making up almost a quarter of all 323,000 backpacker visas issued last year, his government wants the free trade deal to be revisited."Many Brits don't treat it as a working holiday anymore. It's more a three-year career break," says Dan McConnell, general manager of the Mad Monkey backpacker hostel chain.He says Brits used to be the largest clientele at its Cairns accommodation but "now French outnumber British three to one"."We see the Brits get to Sydney, decide it's the coolest place in the world, and stay there," he adds.It's a privilege not enjoyed by working holidaymakers from other countries who must do at least 88 days of "specified regional work" in industries that need a seasonal or temporary workforce - including agriculture, fisheries, tourism and hospitality - if they want to qualify for a second year extension, and six months to stay a third year.Barely a month ago, Albanese ruled out forcing British backpackers to do the same, accepting it as part of the trade deal.But, under pressure from businesses here in Far North Queensland and other regional Australian communities, who are concerned about a lack of labour, the mood music has changed.Last week Albanese met UK counterpart Andy Burnham at the meeting of Commonwealth leaders in the Caribbean.And alongside AI, gender violence online and the AUKUS defence pact, backpackers were on the agenda.Despite speculation in the Australian media, no immediate announcement was made. Albanese instead told reporters that he had pushed for a change in the rules on backpackers and that Burnham had been "very constructive about it"."We'll work those issues through over coming weeks," he said adding that the free trade agreement was not set in stone and tweaks could be made "if there are good policy reasons".Backpackers make up one in seven farm jobs across Australia, with about 52,000 people on working holiday visas doing jobs in horticulture each year, according to the National Farmers Federation.It welcomed Albanese's discussions with Burnham, but said the issue of worker shortages in agriculture was far broader than the UK deal.Of greater concern are wider proposals, announced in September, to cut net migration into Australia, under political pressure from the resurgent right wing populist One Nation party and the opposition coalition.That includes an overhaul of the working holiday visa system, introducing a ballot for backpackers wanting to extend their stay – capped at 45,000 for people wanting a second year in Australia (down from 57,000 who qualified this year) and just 5,000 allowed to remain for a third year (compared with 31,000 this year).This, the federation says, is "a low blow".Those plans are still out for consultation, but immigration officials have slowed processing rates for some working holiday visa applications and paused them from several countries.Tourism Tropical North Queensland chief executive Mark Olsen has also been among those lobbying Albanese in Canberra - telling him that backpackers brought both the spending power and the temporary labour needed to fill seasonal roles in a region famed as a gateway to the Great Barrier Reef and the Unesco world heritage listed Daintree rainforest.Young Brits temporarily living and working in this region peaked at around 20,000 he says. Now it's closer to 11,000."Numbers have dropped significantly since the UK free trade agreement kicked in when border arrangements returned to normal [after the pandemic] in 2023 ," he said.Cairns restaurateur Fintan Rafferty says that of about 180 staff on his payroll across four venues, only five are British. Prior to the visa rule change, that was closer to 25.UK workers came with good skills in hospitality and "were willing to work, and to work flexible hours", he told the BBC.And, he said, it was a two-way street. "The pay is very good, the conditions are very good. And one of the great things about the 88-days rule is that it forces people to travel. It's enriching their experience."Bucking the trend, at the bar of Gilligan's backpackers, Paige Tomlinson serves vodka and soda with plenty of ice and a broad South Yorkshire accent.The 27-year-old, from Barnsley, has been in Cairns for four months, attracted by the "chilled" lifestyle and local waterfalls."Most people prefer Sydney and they question me all the time why I'm here," she laughs. "But I got to Sydney and I just didn't like it. It was too busy, too much like London and I don't like London."She says she'd like to see the regional work requirement brought in for all Brits,  "getting them out their comfort zone"."If every other country's got to do it, why should we not?"About 200km north, at  Red Valley Farm in Lakeland, general manger Peter Inderbitzen agrees.Workers mainly from Tonga, hired on a Pacific labour scheme, pick bananas there year-round.But Inderbitzen also relies heavily on backpackers, especially at peak avocado season, employing about 25 people for a couple of months each year."It's very short, sharp, get it done, get it out kind of work," he told the BBC. "But without those pickers, the avos stay on the tree."While a few British backpackers were still applying for work, numbers had "completely dropped off" since the rule change, said Inderbitzen, who'd "love" to see British travellers having an incentive to head to the regions."As much as it wasn't perfect, [that programme] was working."Back in Cairns, most of the young Brits the BBC tracks down are on tourist visas - but many want to return for a working holiday.Among them is Ethan Phillips, 23, from Buckinghamshire who has been having way too much fun to keep up to date with what politicians have been discussing."It makes sense for them to want us to do [regional work] again," he says. "I mean I'd rather not do it, but if we have to, it's only three months … it can't be that bad."

schema.headline: Why does Australia want Brits to swap Sydney for the outback?

title: Russia-Ukraine talks turn to post-war security but end without breakthrough
description: Trilateral talks in Abu Dhabi between Russia, Ukraine and the US aimed at ending the war in Ukraine have concluded after a second day.Although the Ame
body: Trilateral talks in Abu Dhabi between Russia, Ukraine and the US aimed at ending the war in Ukraine have concluded after a second day.Although the American side said they saw "some openings", there was no hint of any breakthroughs to end the nearly five year-long war sparked by Russia's invasion.However, both Moscow and Kyiv confirmed that a large-scale prisoner of war exchange was in the works and could be carried out soon. Davyd Arakhamia from Ukraine's negotiating team said that this round of talks - the first since February - "was one of the hardest.""I believe the Russians came with very strict directives, so it was extremely difficult to soften the discussion," he said. But he added that he felt "good momentum" and urged for a second round of talks to be organised as soon as possible. Comments by Kremlin negotiator Vladimir Medinsky were less conciliatory. "Right now... a lot depends on Ukraine, on the position of the US, and on whether Europe comes to its senses," he said. After the talks it was announced that on Thursday US negotiators Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner - President Donald Trump's son-in-law - would travel to Moscow to meet Russian President Vladimir Putin, and then to Dublin to speak to Ukraine's Volodymyr Zelensky. The meetings in Abu Dhabi had been framed as centred around the "security architecture" of Europe.For Kyiv, this may include reassurances that allies will come to its aid if Ukraine comes under attack again, despite the country not being a Nato member. For Moscow, a reworked "security framework" is likely to include a limit to the influence of Nato in eastern Europe - a central concern for the Kremlin since the alliance's eastward expansion.Earlier this week Kushner said the US hoped to "create a new framework" of security between Ukraine, Russia and Europe that could "secure lasting peace", while the Kremlin's Medinsky said the world needed a "new" and "fair" security system.That framework would serve as "a new Yalta and Potsdam", Medinsky said, referring to the 1940s summits in which the victorious Allied powers carved up post-war Europe into spheres of influence. Ukraine and Europe have long been concerned about the current US administration's commitment to European security and its softening towards the Kremlin. Representatives of Britain, Nato and various EU countries were also in Abu Dhabi and met with US and Ukrainian negotiators, but the Kremlin - with whom the EU does not officially communicate - said its delegation had not had any contact with them. Moscow has been dismissive of European involvement, although Europeans have long argued that they are central to any post-war dynamics on their continent.Many - particularly in eastern Europe - feel their security is linked to that of Ukraine. Agreements cannot be implemented "if no consensus can be reached among Nato members," a German government spokesperson said on Wednesday.Kushner said the US was keen to bring the Europeans on board and said that getting them "added to the format" would be on the agenda for his talks with Putin.There is also disagreement on whether discussions on a future security framework should be preceded by a ceasefire, as the Europeans and Kyiv would want, or whether the fighting only stops after an agreement has been reached, as the Kremlin has insisted.Any agreement on a peacetime security framework, however, is contingent on the war ending, Kushner noted. But that cannot occur "until there's an agreement on territory and on all other bilateral issues," he added.Since talks began last year, a core obstacle to any settlement has been Ukraine's eastern region of Donetsk, which is mostly occupied by Russia. Kyiv wants to freeze the contact line to maintain control over those areas, which it says are essential to its security. Moscow, meanwhile, has never backed down from its demand that Ukraine relinquish the parts of Donetsk it still holds. "Every inch" of land would be "returned to Russia one way or another", Medinsky said.Kushner acknowledged that the territorial question remained the hardest, while Zelensky's chief of staff and negotiator Kyrylo Budanov refused to be drawn on whether Russia was still demanding a Ukrainian withdrawal from the region.Later, Budanov admitted the talks had been "tough" and that Ukraine's priority was to ensure Russia could not attack it again."These deals are very hard and complex, and this one is very emotional, very complex," Kushner said. "The reality is there is no trust right now between the sides and that is to be expected after a conflict like this."

schema.headline: Russia-Ukraine talks turn to post-war security but end without breakthrough

title: David Walliams: Author Chloe Combi says there were 'real concerns' about him in publishing industry
description: Combi said she was getting invited to events such as book launches around the time one of her own books was being published, and was also running a sc
body: Combi said she was getting invited to events such as book launches around the time one of her own books was being published, and was also running a scheme to bring "high-profile and inspiring writers and speakers" to talk in schools.At an event in 2015, Combi said she got speaking to someone "quite senior" in publishing, who warned her about Walliams. "We were talking about [the scheme] and possible writers who might be good for the project to work well with teenagers," Combi said."She gave me some great recommendations and said to me: 'Whatever you do, don't invite David Walliams, and FYI if you are speaking to head teachers or teachers, please inform them that he's not a good booking, not an appropriate booking for a school'."Combi continued: "I obviously asked why, and to be honest I had already heard quite a lot of rumours because those worlds are quite small and contained."One of the things she said was that there had been real concerns about his behaviour around young female staff."If you are affected by any of the issues in this story, help and support is available at BBC Action Line.Asked whether concerns about his behaviour was an open secret, Combi replied: "Yes definitely... and I'd heard it from people who worked in publishing, fellow writers, people kind of in celebrity and TV circles."Combi said she never met Walliams herself, and said her information had come from "a number of people I was speaking to".HarperCollins in September announced it would no longer be publishing his back catalogue. Earlier on Wednesday, media minister Ian Murray said there is a "cultural problem" in the industry that needs to be "stamped out".Giving evidence to the Digital, Culture, Media and Sport Committee, Murray said he was "deeply saddened and also angry" to see the prevalence of abuse by men in the media industry.Meanwhile, Minister for Women and Equalities Bridget Phillipson paid tribute to the "bravery" of victims who have shared their experiences in recent days.Speaking in the Commons, she said: "Women and girls should never have to shrink our lives or ambitions because of outdated, misogynistic attitudes, and the appalling testimonies we have heard in recent days underline how much further we have to go."Comedian and podcaster Deborah Frances-White told BBC Radio 4's The World at One that young women are "definitely" still being exploited in the comedy industry.She told the programme that perpetrators understand consent but they just enjoy the power that comes with ignoring it, adding: "The thrill is in the contravention of consent."Asked whether she recognised the picture Russell Brand's conviction and allegations against Walliams had painted of the comedy industry, she said: "Yes, entirely."She described an industry where she was asked to meet male producers in darkly lit rooms "walking a tightrope", having to make them feel attractive and avoid being assaulted as they influenced future employment opportunities.She said these events are "definitely still going on" and that she is in a WhatsApp group with female comedians who share their experiences with each other.

schema.headline: David Walliams: Author Chloe Combi says there were 'real concerns' about him in publishing industry

title: Scottish man confirmed as victim of Krakow shooting
description: Image source, FacebookImage caption, James Thomas Campbell is understood to have died in the Krakow shootingUpdated 10 minutes agoA 32-year-old Scotti
body: Image source, FacebookImage caption, James Thomas Campbell is understood to have died in the Krakow shootingUpdated 10 minutes agoA 32-year-old Scottish man has been confirmed as one of the victims of a mass shooting in Poland that left six people dead.The man, who is understood to be James Thomas Campbell from Prestwick in South Ayrshire, died when a lone gunman opened fire in central Krakow on Saturday.Campbell worked as a DJ in Ayrshire. Police Scotland confirmed it was providing specialist support to the victim's family, but formal identification is yet to be carried out.The 24-year-old attacker, named as Michal Oksinski by local media, died in hospital on Monday, having also fatally shot four Polish citizens and an Austrian woman with a further 15 people, including two police officers, injured.Det Ch Insp David McAlinden, senior investigating officer from Police Scotland's Counter Terrorism Policing unit, said the force was "aware of the tragic death of a Scottish man in Krakow".He added: "Working in conjunction with COPFS (the Crown Office and Procurator Fiscal Service), Police Scotland is supporting the UK counter-terrorism policing network and the Polish authorities. "The immediate shared priority is to ensure that identification is properly established for the family, so that repatriation can take place as quickly as possible."The family has asked for their privacy to be respected. Our thoughts are with them and everyone impacted by this incident."Mark Jewell, a close friend of Campbell's who regularly DJ'd with him, described him as "a quiet, kind and soft-hearted person, who wouldn't have harmed a fly".He added: "It's just so tragic that he had to be in the wrong place at the wrong time."I had been speaking with him when he was headed over to Poland and I messaged him as soon as I heard about the terrible attack, to ask if he was safe - not for one minute expecting that he would have been caught up in it all."I was fully expecting a funny message back from him, saying not to worry. I can't quite get my head round it all."Image caption, The attack happened in Krakow on SaturdayThe attack began shortly before 15:00 local time (14:00 GMT) in Krakow's Main Market Square, a popular tourist spot.Police said the gunman drove into the square before beginning to fire at random people from his car.Armed officers raced to the scene and engaged in a gunfight with the man, who was shot within three minutes of the attack beginning.In addition to the six people killed in central Krakow, police later found the bodies of the gunman's parents and sister at his address on Saturday.Earlier this week two friends from Aberdeen described how they ran for their lives as the shooting started.Ciaran McMenemy, 26, and Charlie Hutchison, 27, said they had just sat down for a drink when the gunfire began. They quickly fled and took shelter.

schema.headline: Scottish man confirmed as victim of Krakow shooting

title: Luke Littler: World number one expected 'pub player' opponents on Netflix show
description: Luke Littler has admitted he thought he would be facing pub players on his recent Netflix show, which was billed as giving "amateurs a chance at life-
body: Luke Littler has admitted he thought he would be facing pub players on his recent Netflix show, which was billed as giving "amateurs a chance at life-changing money".Broadcast live globally on the streaming platform last month, the cash was won by top women's player Fallon Sherrock.The format of 'Beat Luke Littler' saw 24 players selected to take on the world number one in a single leg of 501, hoping to win a prize of £501,000.The 24-strong field did include low-level opponents, such as an Australian jockey, a bin man and a Nando's manager, but anyone who was not a member of the PDC Tour was also allowed to compete.That meant Sherrock - who became the first female player to beat a male opponent at the PDC World Championship on her way to the last 32 in December 2019 - and leading junior players Mitchell Lawrie and Zach Griffiths were also eligible."Before I saw the line-up, I thought it was just pub players," said Littler, who is preparing for the Grand Slam of Darts this weekend."Whereas obviously when the line-up came out, I probably knew just over half of them."Mitchell, Zach Griffiths - I played with him on the Development Tour - obviously Fallon, Katie Sheldon and a lot more."I mean Fallon, she's never had a Tour card, so she went for the qualifiers and she made it through. But then she wasn't guaranteed to play - she went in on a vote."Sherrock, who has been awarded an MBE for her services to darts, made it through an audition process and then had to rely on the public to select her to take on Littler at Manchester Central.Littler beat 14 contestants but then lost to Sherrock, who won nearest the bull to throw first and then checked out in 15 darts."It was a very good night overall," Littler added. "I think from my side it was very good. From Netflix's side, it was very good."I think the whole thing was probably a learning curve. For me, constantly playing back-to-back, especially in the heat, I was going off and on stage. I'm up for another one and I'm sure Netflix will be as well."There aren't many people who could say they've got their own show, and I've had my own show on Netflix, which is just still bonkers to me."

schema.headline: Luke Littler: World number one expected 'pub player' opponents on Netflix show

title: Mauricio Pochettino ready to accept Man Utd offer to replace Michael Carrick.
description: Mauricio Pochettino is ready to accept an offer from Manchester United to become their next head coach.United have opened talks with the Argentine abo
body: Mauricio Pochettino is ready to accept an offer from Manchester United to become their next head coach.United have opened talks with the Argentine about him potentially replacing Michael Carrick, who is expected to be relieved of his duties in the next 48 hours.Once Carrick's future is clarified, sources have told BBC Sport that USA manager Pochettino wants to take the job.US Soccer officials are expecting an official approach from United - and sources have told BBC Sport they have a contingency plan for their manager leaving, which includes a succession plan.Former Tottenham and Chelsea boss Pochettino wants to remain respectful to the US Soccer Federation and will wait for United to make their approach.The Red Devils would be required to pay $10m (£7.5m) to release Pochettino from his contract, which he only signed in August.The USA have a two-legged Concacaf Nations League quarter-final against Haiti over the next week. With confidence over a succession plan, it raises the possibility that Pochettino may not take charge of those games.On Thursday, US Soccer cancelled planned media with players citing a clash with Veterans Day, though some reports claimed it was to stop the squad being asked about their manager.Pochettino, 54, is understood to view the prospect of managing United as a serious opportunity, with the expectation being he would accept the job were it formally offered.United have spoken to the ex-Argentina defender about their managerial position on three previous occasions - when Jose Mourinho was sacked in 2018, then in 2022 before the club appointed Erik ten Hag and again when the Dutchman was sacked in 2024.Carrick's future at United will be decided at a meeting in Monaco on Wednesday that will be attended by chief executive Omar Berrada, director of football Jason Wilcox and co-owner Sir Jim Ratcliffe.Berrada and Wilcox have flown to Monaco for one of their regular, planned meetings to discuss strategy around the football club.On this occasion, the main issue to be decided is Carrick's future and what should happen next.It is expected that Berrada and Wilcox's recommendation is for the head coach to go.Carrick, 45, was pictured arriving at the club's Carrington training base on Wednesday.United are 18th in the Premier League - inside the relegation zone - after winning just one of their first 10 games and none since August.It is the club's lowest position at this stage of a top-flight season since 1986-87, when they were 20th.Pochettino's first job in the Premier League was at Southampton from January 2013, before a five-year stint at Tottenham from 2014 that included a Champions League final appearance.He managed Paris St-Germain from January 2021 to July 2022 before spending the 2023-24 season in charge of Chelsea.Pochettino moved into international football by taking the USA job in September 2024, and led the co-hosts to the last 16 of the 2026 World Cup.While it may seem a touch immoral for Manchester United to be talking to a potential new manager before they have decided if their current one is staying or not, this kind of situation is not uncommon in football.Jose Mourinho had agreed a contract with United in 2016 before Louis van Gaal was sacked, which is how stories - including from BBC Sport - came out that the Dutchman would be dismissed as he was celebrating the FA Cup final triumph over Crystal Palace.Going further back, Mark Hughes was replaced immediately by Roberto Mancini at Manchester City in 2009. Hughes' imminent dismissal was reported on the morning of his final game in charge. It is impossible to reach that situation without talks taking place beforehand, and it would be naive to think they do not go on in a world in which agents are pushing clients for jobs that either do, or do not, exist or clubs are trying to gauge interest before making a decision.I have been told by one source the Pochettino terms to join United are more or less agreed. I have also been told if they decide to push on, United can decide whether the former Spurs and Chelsea boss remains with the USA team for their matches against Haiti.If he did stay, it would mean a sharp turnaround from a Tuesday night match - which finishes in the early hours of Wednesday - to be at Carrington for preparations before United's game against Liverpool at Anfield on 22 November.There are a lot of gaps to fill in yet, not least whether Carrick will be dismissed or not.But it seems more likely there will be clarity on that on Wednesday, and from that the rest of the jigsaw pieces should start to slot into place.

schema.headline: Mauricio Pochettino ready to accept Man Utd offer to replace Michael Carrick.

title: England v Japan: Eddie Jones sets sights on chaos and upset
description: Japan want 'the sky to fall in' at Twickenham - JonesImage source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Eddie Jones (left) and Steve Borthwick have worked toget
body: Japan want 'the sky to fall in' at Twickenham - JonesImage source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Eddie Jones (left) and Steve Borthwick have worked together with Japan and England in the pastByBBC Sport rugby union news reporterHead coach Eddie Jones says Japan are drawing inspiration from Italy, who beat England for the first time in March, as the Brave Blossoms attempt to heap pressure back on Steve Borthwick with their own landmark win on Saturday.Jones was sacked by England in December 2022 after a miserable autumn which ended in a 27-13 Twickenham defeat by South Africa and jeers from the home fans.The Australian, 66, hopes to cause similar unrest on his return to Allianz Stadium this weekend."We're massive underdogs," Jones told BBC Radio 5 Live."We've got to find a way to disrupt an England side that's looking at New Zealand next week [England play the All Blacks on 21 November] and sometimes may be a little bit distracted."Our opportunity is to get in there, cause some havoc, cause some chaos, put off their game, get the crowd booing. Then the sky starts to come in on Twickenham and you never know what can happen."We've seen it happen with Italy and other countries."Japan have lost all six of their previous Test meetings with England, most recently going down 54-19 on their autumn visit two years ago.However Italy, who won for the first time in 33 attempts earlier this year, and Fiji, who broke their duck with a 30-22 success in 2023, have both secured maiden victories over England during Borthwick's reign.Jones believes England's players are uniquely susceptible to pressure, given a level of scrutiny which is unprecedented in the rest of the global game.Figure caption, Steve Borthwick is 'an outstanding coach': Eddie JonesA run of five successive defeats earlier this year, combined with reports of a rift between players and coaches, raised the stakes for England before Sunday's meeting with Australia.However, Borthwick's players, who had insisted that the squad remains united, delivered an impressive 45-22 victory to vindicate their coach."The noise does get to the team and it can be pretty loud in England," said Jones, for whom Borthwick worked as an assistant during a previous stint with Japan and then with England."You've got a lot of newspapers, a lot of media, probably more than any other country in the world. Sometimes that can weigh down on the players and it's the job of the leadership to get the players thinking straight."Steve's an outstanding coach and a very intelligent man, and a really good coach. So I've got the highest respect for him."Figure caption, England ease pressure on Borthwick after big win over AustraliaEngland back row Henry Pollock scored two tries after replacing the injured Immanuel Feyi-Waboso on the wing at half-time against Australia, and has been tipped to make only his second start for his country on Saturday.Having also scored a hat-trick off the bench against Fiji in July, Pollock is averaging a try every 22 minutes in the Nations Championship.However, Jones believes the 21-year-old's sky-high strike-rate is not the best measure of him as a player."I wouldn't look too much into it," he said of Pollock's two scores against Australia."Everyone was licking the ice cream on Sunday. They were on the front foot, everyone's lining up to run the ball, there's no pressure in the game."He's a fast back rower, he got the ball in space and he's a talented player, there's no doubt about it, but you couldn't read into it any more than that."Jones is missing his own young star.Fly-half Ryunosuke Ito was plucked from university rugby by Jones, and made his debut against Italy in July without having ever played a professional match.Ito scored his own solo try against Australia in August, neatly stepping through the Wallabies defence., externalImage source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Ito's Test career has been stalled while he completes his obligations to his university teamHowever the 21-year-old fourth-year student, who has established himself as Jones' first-choice fly-half, is required by Meiji University for a collegiate competition, meaning he is missing the northern hemisphere leg of Japan's Nations Championship campaign.Ito will join top-flight Tokyo side Suntory Sungoliath next season, who have former New Zealand captain Sam Cane and Ireland and British and Irish Lions wing James Lowe in their squad."That's the uniqueness of Japanese rugby," added Jones.England v JapanNations ChampionshipSaturday 14 November, 16:40 GMTAllianz Stadium, TwickenhamLive on BBC Radio 5 Live, the BBC Sport website and app

schema.headline: England v Japan: Eddie Jones sets sights on chaos and upset

title: US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent relocated after alleged Iranian threats
description: US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has been moved from his Washington DC home to a military base after Iran-linked threats to his life, according to
body: US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has been moved from his Washington DC home to a military base after Iran-linked threats to his life, according to US media reports. CBS, the BBC's US partner, said the relocation came after a photo of Bessent's home was published in the Wall Street Journal. Bessent has been at the forefront of efforts to isolate Iran economically through sanctions and a wider economic blockade. While the exact nature of the threats against Bessent remain unclear, US intelligence has warned that Iran has "substantially increased" efforts to target Americans, including US officials. "After the Wall Street Journal published an article featuring an online photo that allowed the location of the secretary's Georgetown home to be geo-located, security concerns began to increase," a source told CBS.Georgetown is an affluent part of Washington that is home to a number of government officials and prominent residents. Those security concerns, the source added, prompted authorities to move Bessent to a military base in the area. In a statement, a Treasury Department spokesperson said only that Bessent "will not be deterred" by threats and "remains committed" to the US effort to pressure Iran's economy.The BBC has contacted the White House for comment. In September, Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton warned that Iran has "substantially increased" efforts to target Americans. The New York Times has reported that the Iranian effort includes the targeting of current and former US officials. One source told the newspaper this has "reached a more advanced stage".Other US officials reportedly on Iran's list of potential targets include former Secretary of State Mike Pompeo, former National Security Advisor John Bolton and Mark Milley, the former chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff. Milley and Bolton's security teams were taken away by the Trump administration shortly after he returned to office last year. Bessent is one of a number of administration officials that live on military bases. The White House's new chief of staff, Stephen Miller, was moved to a base in late 2025 - before the conflict with Iran began. Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth and Secretary of State Marco Rubio both live on military bases, as did former Attorney General Pam Bondi and former intelligence chief Tulsi Gabbard. The US and Israel launched an air campaign against Iran in February, killing its leader and prompting the regime in Tehran to retaliate with strikes on US allies across the region and the effective closure of the Strait of Hormuz, through which around a fifth of the world's oil and gas usually travels.In June, the US and Iran reached a preliminary agreement to end the war and reopen the strait, but it collapsed within weeks after Iranian attacks on shipping resumed and the US reinstated a blockade targeting Iranian ports.

schema.headline: US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent relocated after alleged Iranian threats

title: Richmond upon Thames is Britain's happiest place, survey finds
description: Richmond returned to number one after previously winning in 2023 and finishing second last year.Mayor of Richmond upon Thames councillor Nancy Baldwin
body: Richmond returned to number one after previously winning in 2023 and finishing second last year.Mayor of Richmond upon Thames councillor Nancy Baldwin said: "This recognition is especially meaningful because residents highlighted their pride in the local area, our beautiful parks and green spaces, and the local services they rely on every day."Above all, it is our people and communities that make Richmond special."Second-placed Harrogate also ranked highly for access to nature and green spaces.Across Britain, four-fifths (81%) of people who took part in the survey said they were happy with where they live.People took part in the research after being emailed via Rightmove's database, so the survey was self-selecting.Colleen Babcock, a property expert at Rightmove, said: "Richmond stands out for offering a combination many people value: easy access to nature and green spaces, without having to give up local services, places to eat and shop, or employment opportunities."This year's results suggest that the places people rate most highly aren't simply urban or rural, but often bring together some of the best elements of both."

schema.headline: Richmond upon Thames is Britain's happiest place, survey finds

title: What are cold weather payments and who can get them?
description: Image source, Getty ImagesUpdated 6 hours agoAs temperatures drop, heating costs rise, but there is some help for many households through cold weather
body: Image source, Getty ImagesUpdated 6 hours agoAs temperatures drop, heating costs rise, but there is some help for many households through cold weather payments.This financial help is triggered across hundreds of postcodes in England, Wales and Northern Ireland when there is a prolonged period of below-zero temperatures.In Scotland, those on low incomes and benefits may receive a separate winter heating payment, which does not depend on how cold it gets. What are cold weather payments?Who can get cold weather payments and how much are they worth?To qualify, you must live in England, Wales or Northern Ireland.Payments are not age-related but you must already be receiving certain benefits, including:pension creditincome supportincome-based job seekers' allowanceincome-related employment and support allowanceuniversal credit - although there are certain exceptionssupport for mortgage interestEach cold weather payment is for a seven-day period and is worth £25.More than one payment will be made during the course of the winter if there are enough periods of cold weather.The scheme runs between 1 November and 31 March each year.Image source, Getty ImagesHow do I get cold weather payments and how long does it take?You do not have to do anything in order to receive cold weather payments.The money should be paid automatically into the same bank or building society account as your benefits, within two weeks of the qualifying period of cold weather.If you do not receive a payment, you can contact the Pension Service, external or Jobcentre Plus, external.Cold weather payments do not affect other benefits.They are separate to the winter fuel payment, which is worth £100 or £300 depending on your individual circumstances. About nine million pensioners get the Winter Fuel Payment, after a government u-turn over changes to the eligibility rules.

schema.headline: What are cold weather payments and who can get them?
